claims.text: A coupled DFT/MD strategy will predict low phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys more accurately than conventional empirical or mean-field models.
The improved accuracy results from directly capturing atomic-level disorder and anharmonic phonon scattering.
The target alloys are in an as-synthesized, chemically disordered state.
The proposed method couples DFT and MD calculations to compute phonon spectra and thermal-transport properties.
The simulations will cover temperatures from approximately 300 K to 600 K.
Statistically representative sampling of atomic configurations will be used.
The method assumes that the modeled alloys remain single-phase and chemically disordered.
Atomic-level disorder produces local variations in bonding environments.
Atomic-level disorder and local bonding variations enhance anharmonic phonon scattering.
Explicit treatment of electronic structure and vibrational dynamics captures anharmonic effects and scattering events induced by chemical complexity.
Capturing these anharmonic effects and scattering events improves predictions of phonon thermal conductivity.
The coupled method will reduce typical prediction errors from 30–40% to approximately 15–20%.
Current empirical or mean-field models correlate composition with thermal conductivity without explicitly modeling atomic disorder and anharmonic effects.
The method may be less reliable for alloys with significant local ordering or phase separation because typical simulation cells do not fully capture these features.
A diverse alloy set will be synthesized, measured from 300 K to 600 K, and used to compare simulation errors against conventional-model errors.
The hypothesis is falsified if more than half of the tested alloys fail to show the specified error reduction or exhibit systematic deviations beyond the predicted range.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome defines approximately 15–20% as the final error margin, whereas the falsification rule refers to a 15–20% error-margin improvement relative to conventional methods. These are different quantitative criteria.
